“What is it that you cannot understand?”

“Their reasons for behaving as they do. But I shall tell you everything just as it happened. When I arrived, Mr. Rucastle met me here and drove me in his dog-cart to the Copper Beeches. As he said, it is beautifully situated, though the house itself is not beautiful: a large, square, whitewashed building, stained and streaked by damp and bad weather. It stands in its own grounds, with woods on three sides and, on the fourth, a field sloping down to the Southampton high road, which curves past about a hundred yards from the front door. This land in front belongs to the house, but the surrounding woods are part of Lord Southerton’s game preserves. A clump of copper beeches immediately outside the hall door gives the place its name.

“My employer was as pleasant as ever during the drive, and that evening he introduced me to his wife and child. The explanation we thought probable in your rooms at Baker Street was quite wrong, Mr. Holmes. Mrs. Rucastle is not mad. I found her a quiet, pale-faced woman, much younger than her husband. I should judge her no more than thirty, while he can scarcely be under forty-five. From their conversation I gathered that they have been married about seven years; that he was a widower; and that his only child by his first wife was the daughter who has gone to Philadelphia. Mr. Rucastle told me privately that she had left because she had an unreasonable dislike of her stepmother. As the daughter must have been at least twenty, I can readily imagine that living with her father’s young wife had been uncomfortable for her.

“Mrs. Rucastle seemed as colourless in mind as in appearance. She made neither a favourable nor an unfavourable impression on me; she had no presence at all. It was plain that she was passionately devoted to both her husband and her little son. Her pale grey eyes moved constantly between them, noticing every small need and, whenever possible, anticipating it. He too was kind to her, in his blunt, boisterous way, and on the whole they seemed a happy couple. Yet this woman had some secret sorrow. She would often fall into deep thought, with the saddest expression on her face. More than once I have come upon her in tears. I have sometimes thought her child’s nature was weighing on her mind, for I have never known such an utterly spoiled and ill-tempered little creature. He is small for his age, with a disproportionately large head. His entire life seems to alternate between savage fits of rage and dark spells of sulking. His sole idea of amusement seems to be hurting any creature weaker than himself, and he shows remarkable ingenuity in devising ways to catch mice, small birds and insects. But I would rather not speak of the creature, Mr. Holmes; indeed, he has little to do with my story.”
“I welcome every detail,” my friend observed, “whether or not it seems relevant to you.”

“I shall try not to leave out anything important. One unpleasant feature of the house struck me immediately: the servants’ appearance and behaviour. There are only two, a man and his wife. Toller, as he is called, is a rough, uncouth man, with greying hair and whiskers and a constant smell of drink. Twice since my arrival he has been thoroughly drunk, yet Mr. Rucastle appeared not to notice. His wife is very tall and strong, with a sour face. She is as silent as Mrs. Rucastle and much less pleasant. They are a most disagreeable couple, but fortunately I spend most of my time in the nursery and my own bedroom, which stand next to each other in one corner of the house.
“For the first two days after I reached the Copper Beeches, my life was very quiet. On the third, just after breakfast, Mrs. Rucastle came downstairs and whispered something to her husband.

“‘Oh, yes,’ he said, turning to me. ‘We are very grateful to you, Miss Hunter, for indulging our whims to the extent of cutting your hair. I assure you that it has not harmed your appearance in the slightest. Now we shall see how the electric-blue dress suits you. You will find it laid out on the bed in your room, and we should both be extremely grateful if you would be kind enough to put it on.’

“The dress waiting for me was an unusual shade of blue. The material was excellent, a kind of beige fabric, but it showed unmistakable signs of previous wear. It could not have fitted better if it had been made to my measurements. Both Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle expressed delight at its appearance with an enthusiasm that seemed quite excessive. They were waiting in the drawing-room, a very large room running along the whole front of the house, with three long windows extending down to the floor. A chair stood close to the middle window, with its back towards the glass. They asked me to sit there. Then Mr. Rucastle, pacing the other side of the room, began telling some of the funniest stories I have ever heard. You cannot imagine how comical he was; I laughed until I was quite exhausted. Mrs. Rucastle, however, evidently has no sense of humour. She did not even smile, but sat with her hands in her lap and a sad, anxious expression. After an hour or so, Mr. Rucastle suddenly said it was time to begin the day’s duties, and that I could change my dress and join little Edward in the nursery.

“Two days later we repeated the performance in exactly the same circumstances. Once again I changed my dress, sat by the window and laughed heartily at the amusing stories of which my employer possessed an immense store, and which he told with unequalled skill. Then he handed me a yellow-backed novel and moved my chair a little sideways, so that my own shadow would not fall across the page. He asked me to read aloud to him. I read for about ten minutes, starting in the middle of a chapter. Then, abruptly, in the middle of a sentence, he ordered me to stop and change my dress.

“You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how curious I became about the meaning of this extraordinary performance. I noticed that they always took great care to keep my face turned away from the window, until I was consumed by a desire to see what was happening behind me. At first this seemed impossible, but I soon found a way. My hand-mirror had broken, and a happy thought struck me: I concealed a piece of its glass in my handkerchief. On the next occasion, while I was laughing, I raised my handkerchief to my eyes and, with a little adjustment, could see everything behind me. I confess I was disappointed. There was nothing there. At least, that was my first impression. At a second glance, however, I saw a man standing in the Southampton Road—a small, bearded man in a grey suit, who seemed to be looking towards me. It is a busy main road, with people usually passing along it. This man, however, was leaning against the railings bordering our field and looking intently up at the house. I lowered my handkerchief and glanced at Mrs. Rucastle. Her eyes were fixed on me in a most searching stare. She said nothing, but I am convinced she had guessed that I held a mirror and had seen what was behind me. She got up at once.
“‘Jephro,’ she said, ‘there is an impertinent man out on the road, staring up at Miss Hunter.’
“‘He is not a friend of yours, Miss Hunter?’ he asked.
“‘No, I do not know anyone in this neighbourhood.’
“‘Dear me! How very rude! Please turn round and gesture to him to go away.’
“‘Surely it would be better to ignore him altogether?’
“‘No, no; then he would always be hanging about here. Please turn round and wave him away, like this.’

“I obeyed, and at that very moment Mrs. Rucastle pulled down the blind. This was a week ago. Since then I have neither sat by the window again nor worn the blue dress, and I have not seen the man in the road.”
“Please go on,” said Holmes. “Your account promises to be extremely interesting.”

“I am afraid you will find it rather disconnected, and there may turn out to be little connection between the separate incidents I describe. On my very first day at the Copper Beeches, Mr. Rucastle took me to a small outbuilding near the kitchen door. As we approached, I heard the sharp rattle of a chain and what sounded like a large animal moving about inside.
“‘Look in here!’ said Mr. Rucastle, pointing out a gap between two planks. ‘Isn’t he a beauty?’
“I peered through and made out two glowing eyes and an indistinct shape huddled in the darkness.

“‘Don’t be afraid,’ my employer said, laughing at the way I had started. ‘It is only Carlo, my mastiff. I call him mine, but old Toller, my groom, is really the only man who can manage him. We feed him once a day, and not too much even then, so he is always as keen as mustard. Toller turns him loose every night, and God help any trespasser he sinks his teeth into. For goodness’ sake, never step outside after dark on any pretext whatever: your very life would be at risk.’

“The warning was no empty one. Two nights later I happened to look out of my bedroom window at about two in the morning. It was a beautiful moonlit night; the lawn before the house shone silver, almost as bright as day. I stood absorbed in the peaceful beauty of the scene when I noticed something moving in the shadow of the copper beeches. As it came into the moonlight, I saw what it was. A gigantic dog, as large as a calf, with a tawny coat, hanging jowls, black muzzle and enormous protruding bones. It walked slowly across the lawn and disappeared into the shadows on the other side. That dreadful guard chilled my heart in a way I do not think any burglar could have done.

“Now I must tell you of a very strange experience. As you know, I had cut off my hair in London and placed it in a large coil at the bottom of my trunk. One evening, after the child had gone to bed, I amused myself by examining the furniture in my room and rearranging my few possessions. There was an old chest of drawers: the two upper drawers were empty and open, but the bottom one was locked. I had filled the first two with my linen, and as I still had many things to put away, I was naturally annoyed at being unable to use the third. It occurred to me that it might have been locked by mistake, so I took out my bunch of keys and tried to open it. The very first key fitted perfectly, and I pulled the drawer open. It contained only one thing, but I am certain you would never guess what that was. It was my coil of hair.

“I picked it up and examined it. It had the same unusual colour and the same thickness. Then the impossibility of it struck me. How could my hair have been locked inside that drawer? With trembling hands I opened my trunk, emptied it and took my own hair from the bottom. I laid the two locks side by side, and I assure you they were identical. Was it not extraordinary? However much I puzzled over it, I could make nothing of its meaning. I put the strange hair back into the drawer and said nothing to the Rucastles, feeling that I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer they had locked.

“I am naturally observant, as you may have noticed, Mr. Holmes, and I soon had a fairly accurate plan of the whole house in my mind. One wing, however, appeared entirely unoccupied. Its entrance faced the door to the Tollers’ quarters, but it was always locked. One day, as I came upstairs, I met Mr. Rucastle coming out of this door with his keys in his hand. His expression made him quite a different person from the round, jovial man I knew. His cheeks were red, his forehead wrinkled with anger, and the veins at his temples bulged with passion. He locked the door and hurried past without a word or a glance at me.

“This aroused my curiosity. When I took the child for a walk in the grounds, I went round to the side where I could see the windows in this part of the house. There were four in a row: three merely dirty, while the fourth was shuttered. They were evidently all deserted. As I walked up and down, occasionally glancing at them, Mr. Rucastle came out to join me, looking as cheerful and jovial as ever.
“‘Ah!’ he said. ‘You must not think me rude for passing without a word, my dear young lady. My mind was occupied with business.’
“I assured him I had taken no offence. ‘By the way,’ I said, ‘you seem to have quite a number of spare rooms up there, and one has its shutters closed.’
“He seemed surprised and, I thought, a little startled by my observation.

“‘Photography is one of my hobbies,’ he said. ‘I have set up my darkroom there. But dear me! What an observant young lady we have found! Who would have thought it? Who could ever have thought it?’ His tone was joking, but there was no joke in his eyes as he looked at me. I could read suspicion and annoyance there, but no amusement.

“Well, Mr. Holmes, from the moment I realised there was something about those rooms that I was not supposed to know, I burned to explore them. It was not simply curiosity, though I have my share of that. It was more a sense of duty—a feeling that some good might come from finding my way inside. People speak of women’s instinct; perhaps that was what gave me the feeling. Whatever it was, I felt it, and I watched eagerly for any opportunity to go through the forbidden door.

“The opportunity came only yesterday. I should tell you that, besides Mr. Rucastle, both Toller and his wife have some business in these deserted rooms. Once I saw Toller carrying a large black linen bag through the door. Lately he has been drinking heavily, and yesterday evening he was very drunk. When I came upstairs, the key was in the door. I have no doubt whatever that he had left it there. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle were both downstairs, with the child, so I had an excellent opportunity. I quietly turned the key in the lock, opened the door and slipped inside.

“Ahead of me was a short passage, with neither wallpaper nor carpet, turning at a right angle at the far end. Around the corner stood three doors in a row, the first and third open. Each led into an empty, dusty, cheerless room, one with two windows and the other with one. The glass was so dirty that the evening light barely glimmered through. The middle door was closed. Across its outside someone had fixed a broad bar from an iron bed, padlocked at one end to a ring in the wall and secured at the other with strong cord. The door itself was locked too, and there was no key. This barricaded door clearly matched the shuttered window outside, yet the gleam beneath it showed that the room was not dark. Evidently a skylight admitted light from above. As I stood in the passage, staring at that sinister door and wondering what secret it concealed, I suddenly heard footsteps inside and saw a shadow passing back and forth across the narrow strip of dim light beneath the door. A wild, irrational terror overwhelmed me, Mr. Holmes. My strained nerves suddenly gave way. I turned and ran—ran as though some dreadful hand were reaching from behind to clutch the skirt of my dress. I rushed along the passage, through the door and straight into the arms of Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting outside.
“‘So,’ he said with a smile, ‘it was you after all. I thought it must be when I saw the open door.’
“‘Oh, I am terribly frightened!’ I gasped.
“‘My dear young lady! My dear young lady!’ You cannot imagine how gentle and soothing his manner was. ‘And what has frightened you, my dear young lady?’
“But his voice was a little too persuasive. He overplayed the kindness, and I was very much on my guard.
“‘I was foolish enough to enter the empty wing,’ I replied. ‘But it is so lonely and eerie in this faint light that I grew frightened and ran out again. Oh, it is so dreadfully quiet in there!’
“‘Nothing more than that?’ he asked, studying me intently.
“‘Why, what else did you imagine?’ I asked.
“‘Why do you suppose I keep this door locked?’
“‘I am quite sure I do not know.’
“‘To keep out people who have no business inside. Do you understand?’ He was still smiling with the greatest apparent good nature.
“‘I am sure that if I had known—’

“‘Well, now you do know. And if you ever step across that threshold again’—in an instant his smile hardened into a furious grin, and he glared down at me with a demon’s face—‘I shall throw you to the mastiff.’

“I was so terrified that I cannot say what I did. I suppose I rushed past him to my room. I remember nothing until I found myself lying on my bed, shaking all over. Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not remain there any longer without advice. I feared the house, the man, the woman, the servants—even the child. Every one of them horrified me. If only I could bring you down, everything would be well. Of course I could have fled the house, but my curiosity was almost as powerful as my fear. I soon decided what to do: I would send you a telegram. I put on my hat and cloak, walked to the office, about half a mile from the house, and returned feeling much more at ease. As I approached the door, a dreadful doubt struck me: might the dog be loose? Then I remembered that Toller had drunk himself unconscious that evening. I knew he was the only person in the household who had any influence over the savage creature or would dare release it. I slipped safely inside and lay awake half the night, delighted at the prospect of seeing you. I easily obtained leave to come to Winchester this morning, but I must return before three. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are going visiting and will be out all evening, so I must look after the child. Now you have heard all my adventures, Mr. Holmes. I should be very grateful if you could tell me what it all means and, above all, what I ought to do.”
Holmes and I had listened, spellbound, to this extraordinary account. My friend now rose and paced the room with his hands in his pockets and an expression of the deepest seriousness on his face.
“Is Toller still drunk at present?” he asked.
